knowledge.about: Morphism turns your questions into answers you can see and understand on the map — presented as "New Experiences by Moldable Studio". Instead of learning tools and layers, you state a goal in plain language and the system handles the steps. The talk shows it as Morphism in practice: making the design principles tangible, testable and demonstrable.
knowledge.problem: The talk opens with this: maps are powerful tools, but access to their knowledge remains unequal, because the path from question to answer still demands skills many users do not possess. On a traditional flood portal, answering just one question takes 9+ clicks.
knowledge.friction: The talk identifies 4 sources of friction and their cognitive costs: 01 Layer Complexity, 02 Temporal Filtering, 03 Tool Activation, and 04 Spatial Analysis. Together they are the "too much data and too little time" problem — the data is there, but getting from a question to an answer costs too much effort.
knowledge.whyNotAi: Because asking an AI directly is not reliable enough yet. The talk shows geospatial-reasoning accuracy from 2024 to 2026: Claude 3.5 S on MapEval 66%, o4-mini on GeoBenchX 60%, GPT-5-mini on GPSBench 74% — against a human baseline of about 87%. So instead of assuming a trustworthy model, Morphism starts from Trust-Calibrated Design: it assumes models may not always be trustworthy, aims for appropriate reliance on AI rather than maximum automation, and treats trust calibration — not just task success — as a key outcome.
knowledge.goalCentric: Goal-Centric Input is the first design principle: users state their goals and the system plans the necessary steps. Its theoretical grounding in the talk is narrowing the Gulf of Execution — the distance between what you want and the actions a tool makes you perform.
knowledge.constrainedAi: Constrained AI is the second design principle: the model may plan and invoke tools, but it does not generate answers independently. The talk calls this a Deterministic Trust Boundary — at "The Gate", answering the question directly is blocked because it may result in fabricated coordinates, facts or unsupported claims; invoking deterministic tools is what's allowed.
knowledge.legibleReasoning: Legible Reasoning is the third design principle: expose the steps, evidence and sources behind each answer. It supports trust calibration — you can watch what the system is doing and why at each step, instead of being handed a result you cannot check.
knowledge.reversibleControl: Reversible Control is the fourth design principle: users can undo, revise, or return to manual control at any time. It is grounded in direct manipulation and user agency — control matters because the system is designed for appropriate reliance, not blind trust, so you must always be able to step back in.
knowledge.principles: The talk presents four principles, each grounded in theory: 01 Goal-Centric Input — users state their goals, the system plans the necessary steps (narrowing the Gulf of Execution); 02 Constrained AI — the model may plan and invoke tools, but it does not generate answers independently (deterministic trust boundary); 03 Legible Reasoning — expose the steps, evidence and sources behind each answer (supporting trust calibration); 04 Reversible Control — users can undo, revise, or return to manual control at any time (direct manipulation · user agency).
knowledge.aiRole: Planning is allowed, answering is not. The LLM interprets your intent and plans actions — then hits "The Gate": answering the question directly is blocked, because it may result in fabricated coordinates, facts or unsupported claims. What is allowed is invoking deterministic tools (Turf.js · PostGIS) which return verifiable results. So no, the AI does not calculate the spatial answer itself.
knowledge.architecture: The flow presented is: Natural Language → LLM Interprets → Function Calling → Map-Based Answers. You express what you need in familiar terms without learning the tools; the LLM transforms your intent into an executable sequence of actions; function calling invokes deterministic tools to carry out the analysis; and results are presented directly on the map in a form that supports decision-making. Underneath are three layers sharing one tool registry: the Browser Layer (conversation, MapLibre canvas, streamed execution steps, undo support), the Agent Layer (LLM — interpret intent, plan actions, invoke deterministic tools), and Deterministic Tools & Open Data (Turf.js · PostGIS · PMTiles · GeoJSON · STAC).
knowledge.interface: The interface has five annotated parts: 01 Chat Panel — type a question or choose a suggested prompt to get started; 02 AI Context — shows the data and context the AI is currently using; 03 Process Steps — follow what the system is doing and why at each step; 04 Time Filter — shows the time range of the data currently in use; 05 Layer Panel — view and manage the map layers at any time.
knowledge.features: Five features define the design: Answers on the map — results live in the spatial medium, the map itself is the answer (display, not describe); Reasoning you can watch (transparency); AI clearly labelled (provenance); Everything reversible (direct manipulation); and Manual controls kept (agency).
knowledge.demos: Three questions, three demos — each shown side by side, traditional portal versus Morphism: 01 "Where were the flooded areas on 13 October 2025?" (find data → add layer → choose date); 02 "When did the flooding happen?" (understand time range → find dates → show time filter); 03 "How has flooding changed over time?" (compare dates → split view → measure change).
knowledge.comparison: That is demo 03: "How has flooding changed over time?" — compare dates → split view → measure change. Two periods are loaded and shown side by side with a draggable divider, plus a chart of the flooded area so the change is measured, not just eyeballed. In the live app that chart is a horizontal bar chart, because two periods are independent magnitudes rather than parts of one whole.
knowledge.journey: One goal, two journeys. Traditional: open the web → find → toggle → date → buffer → query → read — 7+ interactions, with effort distributed across the entire process. Morphism: state the goal → verify & proceed — one expression of intent plus a quick verification, so effort shifts from operating the tool to evaluating the result. As the talk puts it: the journey does not simply become shorter — it reallocates user effort from operating the tool to evaluating the outcome.
knowledge.study: 25 people took part, doing 6 map tasks each, with a median session of 19 minutes from start to finish. Most were not map people: 16 of the 25 never or rarely use a web map, 9 had no GIS experience at all, and 9 had never used an AI assistant — this was a test with ordinary users, not GIS professionals. The talk frames it as a formative prototype: how it could be evaluated, what has been observed so far, and what questions remain open.
knowledge.results: Three questions, three answers: 01 Usability — 62% time on task; 02 Cognitive Load — 4 of 4 workload measures lower; 03 User Experience — 83% preferred Morphism overall.
knowledge.cognitiveLoad: On cognitive load, all 4 of 4 workload measures came out lower with Morphism.
knowledge.effort: This is the "How We Expect User Effort to Shift" chart. Traditional: 40% operating tools (clicks, toggles), 20% interpreting overlapping layers, 10% waiting, 30% the actual spatial question. Morphism: 5% operating tools, 10% interpreting layers, 10% waiting, 75% the actual spatial question. The slide states plainly that this is a projected distribution informed by Land Intelligence and Geospatial Ecosystem — not empirical results from Morphism users.
knowledge.limitations: The talk states three limitations honestly, each with how they'll be addressed: the model is scripted in the demo — the interaction is shown, model behaviour is not evaluated → wire the live LLM via the same tool registry; an expressivity ceiling — natural language can't specify many expert, long-tail operations → add hybrid natural language plus direct manipulation; and generalization is unproven — demonstrated for maps only → test other untrusted-AI plus trusted-tool domains.
knowledge.takeaway: This work wasn't about making AI smarter — it was about designing interactions that help people use imperfect AI with confidence. Three takeaways: AI removes complexity, not expertise; let AI plan, let tools act; UX is the hardest part, and the heart. The closing line: "It's not about whether you use AI — it's about how well you design the UX."
knowledge.openSource: Yes — open and yours to build on. The code is at github.com/FY0ung/morphism, and the talk closes with: thank you, the code is on GitHub, please build on it.
knowledge.foss4g: The talk is "Designing Web Map Experiences — Beyond Too Much Data and Too Little Time with Intelligent AI Processing", presented at Foss4G 2026 in Hiroshima by Mayurachat Saechan, UX Engineer at Moldable Studio. It runs in six parts: 01 The Problem, 02 Current Approaches and Their Limitations, 03 Proposed Approach, 04 App Demo, 05 Evaluation and Reflections, 06 Key Takeaways.
